title: The price that earns the most
hook: Charge more, earn more? Up to a point. Find the point.

knows: that a higher price means fewer sales (supply-demand lesson)
that revenue is price times quantity sold
doesNotKnow: that revenue rises and then falls as the price rises
why: each price rise gains on every sale but loses some sales

misconception: A higher price always means more money.
objective: The learner can explain that raising a price gains on each unit still sold but loses some sales, so revenue peaks at a middle price and falls beyond it.

claims.text: With 100 − 10 × price loaves sold a day, $3 earns $210 (70 loaves), $5 earns $250 (50 loaves) and $8 earns $160 (20 loaves).
In this model revenue is highest at $5, of every price from $0 to $10.
Each $1 on the price earns $1 more on every loaf still sold but loses 10 loaves; below $5 the gain is larger, above $5 the lost sales are.
claims.source: R(p + 1) − R(p) = (100 − 10(p + 1)) × 1 − 10p = 90 − 20p: positive for p ≤ 4, negative for p ≥ 5.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: straight-line demand and revenue only; profit would also subtract the cost of each loaf.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation; on a straight demand line revenue peaks at the midpoint, where demand is unit-elastic (Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 5). Shown on the stage chip.

recall.question: A shop raises its price and its revenue falls. What must have happened?
options: It lost so many sales that they outweighed the gain on each sale
Nothing: a higher price always brings more revenue
recall.why: A higher price earns more on each sale but loses some sales. Past the peak, the lost sales outweigh the gain, so revenue falls.
